content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) initiated the Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) in the 1970s as a collaborative effort with the cruise ship industry. This program was designed to assist the cruise ship industry in meeting its responsibility to develop and implement comprehensive sanitation programs aimed at reducing the risk of acute gastroenteritis outbreaks. All vessels with foreign itineraries carrying 13 or more passengers are subject to unannounced inspections twice a year, as well as re-inspections when necessary. From the early 1970s to 1986, the program included inspections of U.S. ports, but portions of the program were terminated by the CDC in 1986. However, due to pressure from the cruise industry and the public, Congress directed the CDC to reinstate the program through specific language in its appropriations. Responsibility for the VSP was transferred to the CDC’s National Center for Environmental Health (NCEH) in 1986. The NCEH conducted a series of public meetings to assess the needs and expectations of both the public and the cruise ship industry. As a result, a restructured program was launched on March 1, 1987. The program began charging fees for inspections and re-inspections, with the fees determined by the size of the vessel. In 1989, the VSP published an Operations Manual based on the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) 1976 model code for food service and the World Health Organization’s Guide to Ship Sanitation. This manual was intended to educate shipboard personnel and support the cruise ship industry in maintaining sanitation standards. By 1998, it became evident that the 1989 version of the VSP Operations Manual required updating. Advances in the FDA Food Code, new scientific knowledge about food safety and protection, and emerging technologies in the cruise ship industry necessitated revisions. Over the next two years, the VSP sought input from representatives of the cruise industry, the general public, the FDA, and the international public health community through public meetings and comments. This collaborative process ensured that the 2000 manual addressed contemporary public health concerns related to cruise ship sanitation. A similar process was followed to update the VSP Operations Manual in 2005 and again in 2011. Although the 2011 manual was in use for nearly six years, advancements in technology, food science, and the emergence of new pathogens required further updates. The VSP 2018 Operations Manual incorporated feedback and corrections from government and private industry partners, as well as the public. The CDC expressed gratitude to all individuals and organizations that contributed comments and participated in the revision process. The VSP remains committed to reviewing and incorporating new information, technology, and input to ensure the Operations Manual remains current. The VSP 2018 Operations Manual reflects over 40 years of successful collaboration between government and industry, benefiting millions of travelers annually.
